config.title: Implement DeepReadonly type

intro.title: Implement DeepReadonly type
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a TypeScript type called DeepReadonly that makes all properties of an object—including nested objects—immutable (read-only). You will learn how to use mapped types and conditional types to recursively traverse and transform object structures. The main technologies involved are TypeScript's type system features like keyof, readonly, and recursive type definitions. By the end, you will understand how to create utility types that enforce immutability at any depth, a key concept for type safety in larger applications.
intro.usecase: The DeepReadonly type is essential in TypeScript applications where you need to guarantee data immutability for safety and predictability. In real-world products like configuration dashboards or admin panels, you often fetch complex nested data structures (user profiles with nested permissions, organizational hierarchies, or multi-level settings objects) that should never be accidentally modified by UI components. By applying DeepReadonly to these data structures, you prevent runtime mutations that could cause inconsistent UI states or bugs, while still allowing TypeScript to provide full type safety and autocomplete during development. This pattern is particularly valuable in React applications with state management libraries, where immutable state updates are required for proper re-rendering and performance optimization.

objectives: Construct a basic Readonly type wrapper for primitive values
Apply conditional types to distinguish between objects and primitives
Implement recursive type mapping for nested object structures
Configure the DeepReadonly type to handle arrays and tuples
Integrate the DeepReadonly type into existing TypeScript interfaces
Manipulate type parameters to create flexible generic implementations
Initialize type constraints to prevent invalid type arguments

steps.title: Understand the concept of DeepReadonly
steps.instruction: Read about the DeepReadonly type concept and understand that it makes all properties of an object (including nested objects) readonly.
steps.hint: DeepReadonly is a utility type that recursively makes all properties of an object immutable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: Understanding a utility type concept
type ReadonlyExample = Readonly<{ name: string }>;
steps.seedCode: // No code needed for this conceptual step
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll understand that DeepReadonly recursively applies readonly to all properties, including nested objects.
successCriteria: You've read and understood the concept of DeepReadonly type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've grasped the concept of DeepReadonly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Review that DeepReadonly applies recursively to nested objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's revisit: DeepReadonly makes all properties (including nested ones) immutable.

steps.title: Create a basic Readonly type
steps.instruction: Create a generic type alias named 'MyReadonly' that wraps any type to make all its properties readonly.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword, a generic parameter like T, and the built-in TypeScript 'readonly' modifier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a simple generic wrapper type
type Box<T> = { value: T };
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a reusable type that makes any object's properties immutable at the type level.
successCriteria: The MyReadonly type is defined as a generic type alias that applies 'readonly' to all properties of T.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your type uses a generic parameter and applies 'readonly' to all properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a generic type alias named MyReadonly that makes properties readonly.

steps.title: Define the DeepReadonly type structure
steps.instruction: Create a type named DeepReadonly that uses conditional types to handle different value types recursively.
steps.hint: Start with 'type DeepReadonly<T> =' and use a conditional type to check if T is an object. You can use 'extends' for the condition.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: A conditional type that checks if a type is an array
type IsArray<T> = T extends any[] ? true : false

steps.expectedOutcome: A DeepReadonly type definition with conditional type structure is created.
successCriteria: The DeepReadonly type is defined with a conditional type that checks if T extends object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using 'type DeepReadonly<T> =' with a conditional type.

steps.title: Handle primitive types in DeepReadonly
steps.instruction: Inside your DeepReadonly type definition, add a conditional type that checks if T is a primitive type (string, number, boolean, symbol, undefined, null) and returns T unchanged for those cases.
steps.hint: You can use a conditional type with a union type check: T extends string | number | boolean | symbol | undefined | null ? T : ...
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: conditional type for primitives
type PrimitiveCheck<T> = T extends string | number | boolean | symbol | undefined | null ? T : never;
steps.expectedOutcome: Your DeepReadonly type will now correctly handle primitive types by returning them as-is instead of trying to make them readonly.
successCriteria: DeepReadonly type includes a conditional check for primitive types that returns T unchanged
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your conditional type syntax. Make sure you're checking for all primitive types and returning T unchanged for those cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: The primitive type handling isn't quite right. Remember to use a conditional type that checks if T extends the union of primitive types, then returns T.

steps.title: Handle arrays in DeepReadonly
steps.instruction: Extend your DeepReadonly type to handle arrays by applying DeepReadonly recursively to each element type.
steps.hint: Use a conditional type to check if T is an array, then map over its element type with DeepReadonly.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: making array elements readonly
type ReadonlyArray<T> = T extends Array<infer U> ? ReadonlyArray<DeepReadonly<U>> : T
steps.expectedOutcome: The DeepReadonly type now correctly makes arrays and their elements readonly.
successCriteria: DeepReadonly type includes a conditional branch for arrays that applies DeepReadonly to element types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the array handling might need adjustment. Ensure you're applying DeepReadonly recursively to element types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The array handling is missing or incorrect. Remember to check if T is an array and apply DeepReadonly to its element type.

steps.title: Review and refine the DeepReadonly implementation
steps.instruction: Review your complete DeepReadonly type implementation and ensure it properly handles all edge cases: primitives, arrays, objects, and functions.
steps.hint: Check that your DeepReadonly type correctly transforms all nested properties to readonly recursively.
steps.analogousExample:
// Reviewing a complete type implementation
type CompleteType<T> = T extends Function ? T : T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: CompleteType<T[K]> } : T;
steps.expectedOutcome: A fully reviewed DeepReadonly type that handles all edge cases properly.
successCriteria: DeepReadonly type correctly handles primitives, arrays, objects, and functions with proper readonly constraints.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
